scope.description: Hand-researched deepening pass for Japanese Mystery of the Fossils and ten rows that carry its fossil, ghost, bird, Mew, and mechanical-hinge structure.
in_scope: Mystery of the Fossils release dossier
not_claiming: complete Mystery of the Fossils scholarship

sources.title: Local Japanese pre-English catalog: Mystery of the Fossils
Pokellector: Mystery of the Fossils expansion
TCGdex API set record: PMCG3 Mystery of the Fossils

claims.text: The local catalog models Mystery of the Fossils as released on June 21, 1997.
The local catalog, Pokellector source snapshot, and TCGdex source snapshot support a 48-row Japanese Mystery of the Fossils checklist.

The Japanese pre-English release map treats Mystery of the Fossils as a Japanese main booster expansion and the Japanese Fossil equivalent, but the catalog preserves it as its own release_family_id separate from English Fossil.
The local symbol-status matrix records Mystery of the Fossils as printing with rarity symbols, so this release must not be used as a Base No Rarity source.
The local attention rows for Mystery of the Fossils include Muk, Moltres, Lapras, Raichu, Zapdos, Gengar, Mew, Aerodactyl, Dragonite, and Mysterious Fossil.
The local artist clusters for Mystery of the Fossils are led by Kagemaru Himeno, Ken Sugimori, Mitsuhiro Arita, Keiji Kinebuchi, and a one-row Miki Tanaka contribution.

Mystery of the Fossils matters because it turns Pokemon's first-year creature world toward buried memory: ancient Pokemon, legendary birds, ghosts, and Mew all share a compact 48-row apparatus where discovery feels both archaeological and mythic.

special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Mystery of the Fossils, Japanese Fossil, 化石の秘密, PMCG3, Mew Fossil, Fossil Dragonite, or Mysterious Fossil.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Preserve the Japanese 48-row release boundary, rarity-symbol context, and local catalog row id before comparing to English Fossil or Base No Rarity.
steps: Preserve release_family_id jp_tcg_mystery_of_the_fossils_19970621 and Japanese release context.
Use the local three-digit row id as catalog coordinate; do not assume the physical card prints that number as an English-style collector number.
Do not collapse this 48-row Japanese release into English Fossil's 62-card Wizards checklist.
Do not treat Mystery of the Fossils as a No Rarity source; the symbol-status matrix marks the release as with-rarity-symbol.
For Mew, Dragonite, Aerodactyl, Gengar, and legendary-bird claims, require the seller scan or graded label to support the exact language/release row rather than importing English Fossil memory.

narrative.human_title: The cave opens under the first year
narrative.why_it_matters: Mystery of the Fossils is smaller than English Fossil and stranger in the hand. It feels like the Japanese release where early Pokemon turns from playground creatures toward buried machinery: fossil evolution, cave ghosts, legendary weather, and Mew as a mythic punctuation mark. The set is not only about old Pokemon. It is about the pleasure of finding a creature world under the one you thought you knew.
not_claiming: complete Mystery of the Fossils history

sources.title: Local Mystery of the Fossils row: Muk 007

claims.text: The local catalog identifies Mystery of the Fossils row 007 as Muk.
The local catalog and TCGdex record Muk row 007 as Rare.
The local catalog credits Muk row 007 to Mitsuhiro Arita.

Muk is one of the cards that keeps Mystery of the Fossils from becoming a clean museum case. Arita gives the set a living stink: the old world is not only bones and relics, it is gas, sludge, and active danger. For agents, Muk is also a reminder that Japanese rarity and holo attention do not need English numbering to matter.
